reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation / GeneReviews
clinicalPearls: Combines an acromelic skeletal phenotype (short stature, short hands and feet, brachydactyly, stiff joints) with characteristic ocular abnormalities
The hallmark eye finding is microspherophakia, a small spherical lens that is prone to dislocation (ectopia lentis), typically inferiorly or into the anterior chamber
Lens abnormality causes lenticular myopia and a high risk of pupillary block and secondary glaucoma, which can threaten sight
Genetically heterogeneous: recessive forms from ADAMTS10 or LTBP2 and dominant forms from FBN1, all affecting the microfibril system
It sits within the acromelic dysplasia family and contrasts with Marfan syndrome, where lens dislocation is usually upward and stature is tall
Joint stiffness and brachydactyly help distinguish it clinically from other causes of ectopia lentis
Ophthalmic management focuses on monitoring for and treating pupillary block glaucoma and managing the dislocated microspherophakic lens
reference.pathophysiology: Weill-Marchesani syndrome is a disorder of the fibrillin microfibril system that supports the ocular zonule and connective tissue. Variants in ADAMTS10, LTBP2 or FBN1 disrupt assembly or regulation of microfibrils, weakening the zonular apparatus so that the lens becomes small, spherical and poorly suspended, predisposing to dislocation and angle-closure glaucoma. The same microfibrillar disturbance and associated dysregulated TGF-beta signalling in the skeleton produce the short stature, brachydactyly and joint stiffness that characterise the acromelic phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Marfan syndrome (ectopia lentis, but tall stature)
Other causes of secondary angle-closure glaucoma
additionalInvestigations: Molecular testing of ADAMTS10, LTBP2 and FBN1, usually via a gene panel
Detailed ophthalmic assessment including slit-lamp examination for microspherophakia and lens position
Intraocular pressure measurement and gonioscopy for angle-closure/glaucoma risk
Skeletal survey for short tubular bones and brachydactyly
Echocardiography where cardiac involvement is suspected
Plasma homocysteine to exclude homocystinuria as a cause of ectopia lentis
redFlags: Acute angle-closure glaucoma from pupillary block by the spherical lens
Anterior dislocation of the lens into the anterior chamber
Progressive visual loss from uncontrolled intraocular pressure
Rapidly rising intraocular pressure requiring urgent ophthalmic intervention
reference.prognosis: General health and life expectancy are usually good, but vision is at significant risk from lens dislocation and secondary glaucoma, so the ophthalmic outcome depends heavily on early detection and careful long-term eye care.
pitfalls: Dilating the pupil without recognising that it can precipitate pupillary block in microspherophakia
Confusing it with Marfan syndrome despite the opposite stature and direction of lens dislocation
Missing homocystinuria as an alternative cause of ectopia lentis
Underestimating the glaucoma risk and deferring intraocular pressure monitoring
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
management: Provide lifelong ophthalmological surveillance of intraocular pressure, lens position and refraction to protect sight
Manage the high risk of pupillary-block glaucoma, avoiding miotics that can worsen block by drawing the small lens forward and using mydriasis or laser peripheral iridotomy as appropriate
Undertake lensectomy for symptomatic ectopia lentis or lens-induced glaucoma, and correct the lenticular myopia optically
Offer physiotherapy for joint stiffness and orthopaedic assessment of the skeletal features
Screen for cardiac involvement with echocardiography
Confirm the genetic subtype and offer genetic counselling, recognising both autosomal recessive (ADAMTS10, LTBP2) and dominant (FBN1) inheritance
Coordinate care across ophthalmology, clinical genetics and paediatrics or general medicine, escalating for an acute painful red eye suggesting angle closure
